literal: Even if one begs saying 'water for a cow', to the tongue, than begging, a disgraceful thing there is not.
translation: Even if one begs for water to quench the thirst of a cow, there is nothing more disgraceful to the tongue than that act of begging.
modern: பசுவுக்குத் தண்ணீர் கொடுங்கள் என்று இரந்து கேட்டாலும், ஒருவனுடைய நாவிற்கு இரந்து கேட்பதை விட இழிவானது வேறு எதுவும் இல்லை.
explanation: This couplet highlights the absolute dread and disgrace of begging, which is the theme of this chapter. Even when begging is done for an extremely noble and selfless cause—such as asking for water to save a thirsty cow—the act of begging itself remains the ultimate disgrace for the tongue that utters the request. The poet uses the example of a cow, traditionally a symbol of virtue and helplessness, to show that no motive, however virtuous, can wash away the inherent indignity of begging. It emphasizes that maintaining one's self-respect and avoiding begging is paramount under all circumstances.
